newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan factions meet for U.N.-brokered peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Afghan factions meet for U.N.-brokered peace talks.

text.p: Feuding Afghan factions met in Islamabad under United Nations auspices on Monday to discuss a ceasefire for war-ravaged Afghanistan, a U.N. official said.
The official gave no details and declined to release the names of the participants in the talks.

The Islamic Taleban militia was expected to be represented by Wakil Ahmad, a Kandahar-based adviser to Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar, along with the ambassador at the Afghan embassy in Islamabad Maasoum Afghani and another diplomat.

They were to meet three nominees of an opposition alliance that has been battling the Taleban north of Kabul and in remote northwestern provinces of Afghanistan since the Islamic militia captured the capital on September 27.

Opposition sources named them as General Paynda (one name), representing northern General Abdul Rashid Dostum, Mohammad Ishaq, an aide to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, and Mohammad Rasul Talib, from a Shi'ite Moslem faction.
U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl was expected to announce the result of the talks later on Monday, U.N. officials said.
The United Nations has been trying to persuade the rival groups to agree to a ceasefire, an exchange of prisoners and the formation of a technical committee to oversee the truce.
Success could lead to a dialogue on other issues such as the formation of a broad-based government, demilitarisation of Kabul and creation of a neutral security force for the city.

The Taleban have said in the past they are ready for a ceasefire and prisoner exchange, but reject the idea of demilitarising Kabul. They also insist that any future government must rule in accordance with Islamic Sharia law.
The opposition has previously demanded agreement on the demilitarisation of Kabul as a condition for a ceasefire.
The Taleban, seeking to spread their fundamentalist vision of Islam across Afghanistan, now hold more than two-thirds of the country after seizing Kabul and deposing president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
